summary: Describes the fundamental requirements for an access control list (ACL) model for the LDAP directory service. It lists what such a model must support, but does not define one itself. It is an informational memo.

plainLanguage.summary: A directory holds information that some people may see and others may not. This is the list of what a good set of keys and locks for it should be able to do.

questions: how should ldap manage access to entries
what must an access control model support
subtitle: What LDAP access control systems must be able to do

tldr.problem: LDAP directory services store information that organizations need to control access to—some users should see certain data while others should not, but LDAP had no standard access control model, making it hard to deploy securely.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC lists fundamental requirements that any LDAP access control model must meet, covering general goals, policy semantics, usability, and how to handle complex scenarios like nested groups.
tldr.outcome: The requirements provide a foundation for access control implementations to ensure consistent, secure, and manageable access to LDAP directories across different implementations.

facts.label: Focus area
facts.value: Access control list (ACL) model for LDAP

today: RFC 2820 is informational and has not been obsoleted. It describes the requirements for LDAP access control but does not specify an implementation. Several LDAP implementations have added access control features, though no single model has become universally standard across all LDAP deployments.

sections.title: Why LDAP Needs Access Control
sections.content:
LDAP is a protocol for accessing directory information—like phone books, employee records, and security groups—across networks. As LDAP became widely deployed across enterprises and the Internet, the need to control who can see and modify what information became critical. Organizations must be able to allow some users to read certain entries while denying access to others, and to grant some users the right to modify data.

At the time this RFC was written, LDAP did not define an access control model. This meant each implementation did it differently, making it hard to deploy LDAP securely and to move directories between different systems. The RFC calls this a critical requirement for the successful deployment of LDAP in the marketplace.
sections.plainLanguage: Directories store secrets. You need a way to say 'this person can see their address but not anyone else's.' Nobody had written down how LDAP should do that.

sections.title: General Goals and Requirements
sections.content:
The requirements start with a major objective: provide a simple but secure, highly efficient access control model for LDAP that works for both Internet and enterprise environments.

General requirements include extensibility (the model should support future features), safety (when uncertain, deny rather than allow), and integration with LDAP (administration must be part of the protocol, and access control information must be an LDAP attribute). The model must support policy overrides at the entry level, control access to individual attributes (not just whole entries), and provide per-user granularity. Administrators must be able to aggregate users into groups or roles to simplify administration.
sections.plainLanguage: The system must be simple to understand, hard to break, and flexible enough to grow. When you are not sure, say no.

sections.title: Policy Semantics and Usability
sections.content:
The RFC specifies requirements for how policies work. More specific policies must override less specific ones (for example, a rule about a single user takes precedence over a rule about a group). Multiple policies of equal specificity should be combined in an easily understood way, such as union or intersection. Newly created entries should be subject to a secure default policy.

Usability is emphasized as a security requirement, not just a nice goal. If the access control system is impossible for administrators to use and understand, the result will be insecure. The system must allow administrators to understand what policy applies to any user and entry, to see where inheritance comes from, and to delegate policy administration for subtrees to other users. It must be possible to deny a subject the right to perform directory operations, to support both default-grant and default-deny semantics (though not simultaneously), and to combine multiple access control entries for the same person in a way that is easy to understand.
sections.plainLanguage: Specific rules win over general ones. The system must make sense to humans, or they will set it up wrong.

sections.title: Policy Attributes and Scope
sections.content:
Access policy should not be expressed in terms of attributes that administrators cannot manage (such as groups whose membership is controlled by another organization). Policies should not depend on easily forged attributes like IP addresses, unless the documentation clearly warns of the implications. Humans should not be required to manage policies based on non-human-readable attributes.

Critically, access policy resolution must not depend on the order of entries in the access control list—the system must be deterministic. Rights management must have no side effects: granting one person access to something must not implicitly grant the same or different access to anyone else. A single policy should be applicable to multiple directory entries even in different subtrees without requiring storage of multiple copies. The scope of an ACL is the subtree it governs, and changing one ACL must not change the policy in a different scope.
sections.plainLanguage: The order of rules should not matter. Giving Alice permission should not secretly give Bob permission too.

sections.title: Practical Administration Features
sections.content:
Administrators must be able to control access to entire subtrees with a single ACL at the subtree root. It must be possible to review the effective access of any user, group, or role to any entry and its attributes, which helps administrators verify they set the correct policy. Traversal rights must be separately controllable from read rights, so users can navigate through directory structure without seeing the entries they pass through. It must be possible to create publicly readable entries that even unauthenticated clients can read.

The system must prevent situations where all users, including administrators, get locked out of the directory through misconfiguration. Administrators must be able to configure whether delegated access control information from superior partitions is accepted or rejected, allowing flexible partitioning of administration. It should be possible for administrators to delegate to users the right to grant additional access control rights on entries they create.
sections.plainLanguage: You should not lock yourself out. You should be able to see who can access what, and to let users help manage what they create.
